files.lesson.md: --- order: 1 unit: pages introduces: [decorator] recipes: [object] title: A page from Python summary: "Make a website whose pages come from Python: each address is a route, and a function gives back its page." language: python hook: "When you type a web address, some code decides which page to send back. In Flask that code is Python." app: # The whole site is served: the Python playground loads Pyodide from ../_pyodide/. (_playground-py names the playground for the clip cache.) command: "node \"$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs\" \"$REPO_ROOT/dist\" 8123 _playground-py" url: "http://127.0.0.1:8123/_playground-py/index.html" ready: Python code layout: full voice: true explainClip: query: { code: "@club.py#predict" } caption: "Each route joins an address to a function; the function's return is the page" say: "Each route joins an address to a function, which returns the page." clip: - caption: text: "@app.route(\"/\") joins the address / to the function home." say: "app dot route, slash, joins the address slash to the function home." - click: Run - expect: { selector: "#addr", value: "/" } - wait: 1500 - caption: text: "Visit /about, and Flask runs about() and sends back what it returns." say: "Visit slash about, and Flask runs the about function, and sends back what it returns." - type: { selector: "#addr", text: "/about" } - press: Enter - expect: { selector: "#addr", value: "/about" } - wait: 2500 --- In HTML & CSS you wrote pages by hand. A **web app** makes its pages with code, so they can change: show the latest sign-ups, answer a form, look things up. **Flask** is a small Python library for this. Each address in the site (`/`, `/about`) is a **route**, and each route has a function that gives back the page as HTML. The first lines (`from flask import Flask` and `app = Flask(__name__)`) set up the app: copy them as they are. In this playground, `app.run()` shows your site in the **App** tab, with an address bar. On a computer it would be a real web server at `http://127.0.0.1:5000`. ## Predict ```step stage: predict code: club.py#predict check: type: predict q: "Someone visits /about. What does the site send back?" options: ["A page with the heading About and \"Everyone is welcome.\"", "The Chess club page", "Both pages, one after the other", "Nothing: about() is never called"] actual: "The About page. @app.route(\"/about\") joins the address /about to the function about(), so Flask calls it and sends back the HTML it returns." ``` The line above each function, starting with `@`, is a **decorator**: it joins a function to an address. Which function answers `/about`? ## Run ```step stage: run code: club.py#run try: { playground: python, starter: "club.py#run", height: 520 } check: { type: reflect, text: "I visited both pages with the links and the address bar, and tried an address that does not exist." } unlocks: [a-flask-route] ``` Run it, then use the links on the page, and type addresses in the bar above it: `/about`, then `/missing`. Change the home page's text and run again. ## Investigate ```step stage: investigate code: club.py#run insight: "A route joins an address to a function; whatever the function returns is the page, built as text." tasks: - check: type: question q: "What does a visitor see at /missing?" options: ["A Not Found page (error 404): no route matches that address", "The home page", "An empty page", "Python stops with an error"] answer: 0 explain: "Flask looks for a route that matches the address. With none, it sends back the standard 404 Not Found page, as every website does." - check: type: question q: "home() builds page with page = page + ... three times. What is the page?" options: ["One piece of HTML text, joined from three parts", "Three separate pages", "A list of three lines", "Only the last part"] answer: 0 explain: "page is text; each line adds more HTML to the end. The browser shows the whole thing as one page." - check: type: bug code: club.py#bug text: "Clicking \"About the club\" shows Not Found, though about() is written. Click the line where the problem is." answer: 11 fault: logic misconception: route-missing explain: "about() has no @app.route(\"/about\") above it, so no address leads to it. A function only becomes a page when a route points to it." ``` ### An address with no route What every site does. ### Building the page Text, joined together. ### Spot the bug A page that cannot be reached. ## Modify ```step stage: modify insight: "A new page is a new route and a function; a link to it is an a tag with its address." try: { playground: python, starter: "club.py#run", height: 520 } tasks: - hint: - "Copy the about route: @app.route(\"/results\"), def results():, and return a heading and a table." - "Add a link to it on the home page: `Results`." check: { type: code, text: "Add a /results page with a table of players and wins, and link to it from the home page.", rules: { contains: ["@app.route(\"/results\")", "href='/results'"] } } - hint: - "visits = 0 before the routes. In home(): global visits, then visits = visits + 1." - "Add the number to the page with str(visits)." check: { type: code, text: "Count how many times the home page has been visited, and show the count on it.", rules: { contains: ["visits = visits + 1"] } } ``` ### A results page Add a `/results` page with a small table of players and their wins (as on the club page in HTML & CSS), and a link to it from the home page. ### A visit counter Count the visits to the home page and show the number on it. Visit it a few times, then press **Run** again: what happens to the count? ## Make: your own site ```step stage: make insight: "Goals only: several routes, each with its own page, linked together." try: { playground: python, starter: "club.py#make", height: 520 } check: { type: code, text: "Make a site with a home page and at least two more pages, linked to each other.", rules: { contains: ["@app.route(\"/\")", "href="], defs: 3 } } ``` Make a small site for a club, a team or a hobby: a home page and at least two more pages, each linking back home. ## Where this leads ```step stage: info diagram: ref: diagrams.mmd#visit alt: "A sequence between the browser and the Flask app. The browser asks for /about. Flask runs the route that matches, about(). about() returns the page to Flask, Flask sends it to the browser, and the browser shows it." caption: "What happens when someone visits /about" role: summary check: type: question q: "The visit counter went back to 0 when you pressed Run. Why?" options: ["visits lives in the running program; a new run starts it again from 0", "Flask deletes old pages", "The browser forgot it", "Counters only work on a real server"] answer: 0 explain: "Variables last only while the program runs. To keep sign-ups or counts, a web app saves them to a file or a database: that comes in Lesson 4." ``` Every web app has this shape: addresses, and code that answers them. Next: build pages from data instead of writing every one by hand. ```code diagrams.mmd#visit sequenceDiagram participant B as Browser participant F as Flask app participant R as about() B->>F: asks for /about F->>R: runs the matching route R-->>F: returns the page F-->>B: sends the page Note over B: shows the page ``` ```teacher summary: Students meet Flask, where each address is a route joined to a function that returns the page as HTML, then add a results page, a visit counter and a small site of their own. time: 50 timing: Predict and Run 10 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 20 min · Make 10 min goals: - I can explain what a route is and how Flask chooses the function for an address. - I can add a page to a Flask app and link to it. - I can explain why a variable in a web app resets when the program runs again. before: > Read the unit primer first. This course runs in the **Python playground** (real Python in the browser, Pyodide), where `app.run()` shows the site in an **App** tab with an address bar; links and forms in the page go back to the app. On a computer, `pip install flask` and `python app.py` serve the same file at `http://127.0.0.1:5000`. Before teaching it, open the site's Check your school page once on a student device at school. A **route** (`@app.route("/about")`, a decorator: the line with `@` above a function) joins an address to a function; the function returns the page as HTML text. An address with no route gives the standard **404 Not Found**. HTML inside Python strings uses single quotes for attributes (`href='/about'`) so they do not end the string. The visit counter uses `global` (from the turtle course) and resets on every Run: variables last only while the program runs, which sets up saving in Lesson 4. running: - "Predict: draw a table on the board: address on the left, function on the right." - "Run: have students type /missing and read the 404 page." - "Investigate: ask what the browser receives: just text, which happens to be HTML." - "Modify: visit the counter page five times, then press Run, and ask why it reset." - "Make: sketch the site's pages and links on paper first." stuck: - see: Not Found for a page they wrote. ask: Is there an @app.route line directly above the function, with the right address? fix: Add @app.route("/results") above def results():. - see: SyntaxError on a line of HTML. ask: Do the quotes inside the HTML match the quotes around the string? fix: "Use single quotes inside: \"About\"." - see: "UnboundLocalError: local variable 'visits' referenced before assignment." ask: Does home() say it is changing the variable outside it? fix: global visits as the first line of home(). stretch: Add a page at /time that shows a different message in the morning and the afternoon (import datetime; datetime.datetime.now().hour). support: Give students the results route with its table, and ask them only to add the link from the home page. leads: Next lesson builds pages from a list of data with a template. Later lessons take form answers, save them to a file and send data as JSON. exit: q: What is a route? a: A link between an address in the site, such as /about, and the Python function that makes that page. explain: > 1. `@app.route("/")` joins the address `/` to the function below it. 2. When someone visits an address, Flask runs its function and sends back what it returns, as the page. 3. An address with no route gets a 404 Not Found page. solutions: step-4#t1: club.py#sol-results step-4#t2: club.py#sol-count step-5: club.py#sol-make struggle: Understanding that the browser asks and the function answers. Ask students to say which function runs for each address before they click. ```
